title: Primary dentition
description: Conditions of the primary teeth in children — from early decay patterns through pulp disease, infection, trauma, and eruption disturbances.

problems.description: Rapid, extensive decay across multiple primary teeth in a very young child, often starting at the upper front teeth.
problems.etiology:
Frequent sugar exposure is the driver. The canonical pattern — nursing-bottle caries — comes from a child falling asleep with a bottle of juice or milk, repeatedly bathing the teeth in a sugar-containing liquid throughout the night [1]. Prolonged on-demand breastfeeding beyond age 2 carries a similar risk [1]. The reason the upper incisors go first is anatomy: they are in direct contact with the pooled liquid, while the mandibular incisors sit under the tongue, sheltered by saliva [1].

The broader term **early childhood caries (ECC)** covers all rampant caries patterns in young children, including those driven by frequent sugar-containing drinks, sugar-based medication given long-term, and reduced salivary flow [2].
problems.presentation:
The child is typically 1–4 years old. The parents may present because of visible brown or black destruction of the upper front teeth, or because the child is refusing food or waking at night in pain. Pain may not be reported reliably — anxious children deny symptoms to avoid treatment [3].

What you will see:

- **Upper primary incisors**: circumferential destruction, often leaving only root stumps at worst [1].
- **Lower primary incisors**: characteristically spared in early cases [1].
- In more severe ECC, the first primary molars are also involved [1].
problems.results:
- **Visual exam**: cavitated enamel or exposed dentine on the upper incisors, sometimes cervical lesions wrapping around the neck of the tooth — the pattern follows where the fluid pools.
- **Radiographs**: bitewings show extent of interproximal involvement, though approximal surfaces of spaced primary teeth may be visible directly. Periapicals show inter-radicular radiolucency if pulp death has occurred.
- **Sensibility testing**: unreliable in primary teeth [4].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The distribution is the tell: upper incisors and upper first molars first, mandibular incisors spared. This is the opposite of adult rampant caries and distinct from normal childhood caries, which typically starts in the occlusal pits of the primary molars.

Compare to:

- **Enamel hypoplasia**: affects multiple teeth by shape or colour from the start, not progressive cavitation.
- **Fluorosis**: symmetric opacities or mottling, not cavitation in a feeding pattern.
- Nursing-bottle caries can co-exist with normal pit-and-fissure caries once primary molars are also involved [2].
problems.treatment:
Two parallel tracks: arrest the cause, manage the damage [2].

**Prevention first:**

- Stop bottle use at bedtime; replace with water.
- Apply sodium fluoride varnish (5%) at least twice a year for all children aged 2 and over; four times a year for children at increased risk [5].
- Recommend 1350–1500 ppm fluoride toothpaste for children up to 10 years of age [6].
- Dietary advice: confine sugar-containing foods and drinks to meal times; avoid prolonged sipping [7].

**Restorative management** depends on the extent of damage:

- Small cavitations: Hall Technique crown (no caries removal required), or selective caries removal plus GIC/composite/RMGIC [8].
- Teeth with high caries risk and intact marginal ridges: Hall crown is the primary tool — it seals in caries rather than excavating it [8].
- Grossly destroyed primary incisors near natural exfoliation: extraction is often the pragmatic choice. Composite strip crowns can restore incisors if worth preserving [9].
- Pulpal involvement: see primary-dentition-002 and primary-dentition-003.

If cooperation fails, refer for treatment under sedation or general anaesthesia [2].
problems.prognosis:
With early intervention and behaviour change the caries rate slows and lesions can arrest. Arrested carious lesions tend to be hard and dark [10]. Without change, the upper incisors are lost early; this has limited occlusal consequence but can affect speech, appearance, and feeding, and sets a pattern of high disease risk going into the permanent dentition.

The single strongest predictor of future caries is prior caries experience — a child with ECC is at increased risk for decay in the permanent teeth [11].

citations.quote: Terms used to describe patterns of early childhood caries (ECC) associated with frequent consumption of a sugar-containing drink, especially from a feeding-bottle. Commonly the child falls asleep with the bottle of juice or milk and suckles during the night. Possibly related to the relatively high levels of lactose in breast milk. Characteristically, starts with the maxillary 1° incisors, but in more severe cases the first 1° molars are also involved. The mandibular incisors are relatively protected by the tongue and saliva.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1517 (nursing-bottle caries)

citations.quote: Severe ECC may also be associated with the prolonged and frequent intake of sugar-based medications; however, both pharmaceutical companies and doctors are more aware of the problem and the number of alternative sugar-free preparations is i. Recent studies have confirmed that ECC may be associated with prolonged breastfeeding beyond age 2yrs. Children >1yr old who suckle frequently during the night may be most at risk.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1518 (severe ECC)

citations.quote: Children are not always reliable in reporting pain, either because they have not yet developed the necessary communication skills or because they wish to avoid dental treatment. For example, an anxious child might not report an exfoliating tooth as painful, until reassured.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children — Assessing for pain and infection

citations.quote: Pulp sensibility tests are unreliable in primary teeth and are therefore not recommended.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines — Injuries in the primary dentition, §1.5

citations.quote: For all children aged 2 years and over, apply sodium fluoride varnish at least twice per year. (Strong recommendation; moderate certainty evidence)
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children — Professionally-delivered interventions, key recommendation

citations.quote: Recommend the use of 1350-1500 ppm fluoride toothpaste for children up to 10 years of age.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children — Toothbrushing

citations.quote: By confining sugar-containing foods and drinks to meal times, the time that teeth are exposed to acid attack is reduced. Therefore 'grazing' sugar-containing foods between meals and sipping soft drinks containing sugar or acid over prolonged periods should be avoided.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children — Dietary advice

citations.quote: Based on the available evidence, the principal strategies for managing caries in the primary dentition are: no caries removal, seal with a crown using the Hall Technique; no caries removal and fissure seal; selective caries removal and restoration (i.e. walls prepared to hard dentine with adequate depth for restorative material, previously known as partial caries removal); pulpotomy.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children — Management of caries in primary teeth, key recommendations

citations.quote: Cellulose acetate crown forms for 1° incisors. Enable restoration of 1° incisors using composite resin.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1512 (composite strip crowns)

citations.quote: Carious lesions that are slowing or arrested tend to be hard to probing and dark in colour. However, some arrested lesions can be light in colour.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children — Assessing risk of progression

citations.quote: Amongst the risk factors listed above, previous caries experience (decayed, missing due to caries or filled teeth) appears to be the more reliable predictors of caries risk.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children — Caries risk assessment

problems.description: Short, sharp pain in a child's back tooth on sweet or cold foods, settling quickly when the trigger is removed. No spontaneous pain.
problems.conditionName: Reversible pulpitis in a primary tooth
problems.etiology:
Inflammation of the pulp triggered by a carious lesion that has reached the dentine but has not yet overwhelmed the pulp. The pulp can still maintain perfusion and recover once the stimulus is removed [1].

The anatomy of primary molars makes this a narrow window. Enamel in primary teeth is only ~1 mm thick — half that of permanent teeth. The pulp horns are proportionately larger and more accentuated, meaning caries reaches the pulp sooner than in permanent teeth [2]. The thin pulpal floor and accessory canals to the furcation mean the infection can spread to the inter-radicular area rapidly if the lesion is not managed [3].
problems.presentation:
The child or parent reports brief pain on cold drinks or sweets that goes away quickly. No pain at rest, no pain on biting. The pain may be reported as 'going away by itself' and the parent may not think it is serious.

On examination: a visible carious lesion, usually in an occlusal or proximal surface. The marginal ridge may still be intact in early cases; if the marginal ridge is broken down, pulpal involvement becomes more likely [4].
problems.results:
- **Sensibility testing**: unreliable in primary teeth [5].
- **Percussion**: negative or equivocal.
- **Mobility**: within normal range for the child's age.
- **Radiograph**: dentinal caries visible, no periapical or inter-radicular radiolucency. No widening of the PDL space.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The question is: **reversible or irreversible?** Oxford's rule: fleeting pain on hot/cold/sweet = reversible; longer-lasting or spontaneous pain = irreversible [6].

In primary teeth the distinction matters for treatment choice — reversible pulpitis can be managed with indirect pulp therapy or sealing, without entering the pulp. Irreversible pulpitis requires pulpotomy or extraction.

Unlike in permanent teeth, the clinical signs are less reliable guides. The pulp state can be difficult to diagnose: one root canal may have died while another remains vital [7], and children's pain reporting is less precise [7].
problems.treatment:
Aim: seal the caries off from the pulp and reassess.

- **Indirect pulp therapy**: for asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic vital primary molars with no pulp exposure after caries removal. Leave firm, affected dentine in the deepest part; restore with GIC/composite or SS crown [8].
- **Hall Technique**: seal the carious lesion under a stainless steel crown without caries removal. Suitable for occlusal and approximal lesions [9].
- If in doubt after temporizing: place a temporary dressing, review 3–7 days later. Resolution of symptoms confirms reversible pulpitis and a definitive restoration can proceed [10].
- **Avoid operative intervention until the child can cooperate**. Minimally invasive approaches reduce the risk of treatment-induced anxiety [9].
problems.prognosis: Remove the stimulus and seal the cavity: the pulp typically settles. If the carious process is not controlled, reversible pulpitis progresses to irreversible pulpitis and then to pulp death — the continuum is driven by unmanaged bacterial ingress [1]. Early management is the safest route to a tooth that exfoliates naturally.

citations.quote: The most common reason for children to experience dental pain is pulpal pathology as a consequence of dental caries. The immune system allows vital dental pulps to cope with some bacterial ingress from a carious lesion through the triggering of an inflammatory response in the region of the pulp closest to the lesion. However, if a progressing carious lesion is not managed, then over time the increasing bacterial infection causes a more extensive and severe inflammatory response in the dental pulp.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children — Causes of dental pain or infection

citations.quote: Enamel in 1° teeth is ~1mm thick, which is half that of 2° teeth. The pulp chamber in 1° teeth is proportionately larger, with more accentuated pulp horns. These features mean that caries will affect the pulp sooner and there is a greater likelihood of pulp exposure during cavity preparation.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraphs 1314–1316 (anatomy of primary teeth)

citations.quote: Thin pulpal floor and accessory canals. This may explain the greater incidence of inter-radicular involvement following pulp death.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1332 (thin pulpal floor and accessory canals)

citations.quote: In 1° molars destruction of the marginal ridge indicates a high probability of pulpal involvement.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1350

citations.quote: Pulp sensibility tests are unreliable in primary teeth and are therefore not recommended.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines — Injuries in the primary dentition, §1.5

citations.quote: Fleeting pain on hot/cold/sweet stimuli = reversible pulpitis. Longer-lasting pain on hot/cold/sweet stimuli &/or spontaneous pain with no initiating factor (? child kept awake) but no mobility, not tender to percussion (TTP) = irreversible pulpitis.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1127 (diagnosis of pulpal states in children)

citations.quote: The ∆ of the state of the pulp can be difficult, as not only is a child's perception of pain less precise than an adult's, but the clinical picture may also be complicated by death of one root canal while the other(s) remain vital.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1531

citations.quote: Indicated for asymptomatic, vital 1° molars with no pulp exposure after removal of all soft caries. Leaving carious, but firm, affected dentine in vital, asymptomatic 1° molars has been shown to be reasonably successful.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraphs 1544–1546 (indirect pulp Rx)

citations.quote: For a child with a carious lesion in a primary tooth, choose the least invasive, feasible caries management strategy, taking into account: the time to exfoliation, the site and extent of the lesion, the risk of pain or infection, the absence or presence of infection, preservation of tooth structure, the number of teeth affected, avoidance of treatment-induced anxiety. (Strong recommendation; low certainty evidence)
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children — Management of caries in primary teeth, key recommendation

citations.quote: For both primary and permanent teeth, where there are symptoms of pain that may be due to food packing or pulpitis with reversible symptoms but the diagnosis is uncertain, place a temporary dressing and review the patient 3-7 days later to check symptoms. Resolution of the symptoms at review will indicate that the pulpitis was reversible and a suitable restoration or crown can be placed.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children — Managing dental pain or infection

problems.description: Spontaneous or persistent toothache in a child's back tooth, often keeping them awake. No clear trigger, or pain that lingers long after a cold stimulus.
problems.conditionName: Irreversible pulpitis in a primary tooth
problems.etiology:
Bacterial infection has progressed beyond what the pulp's blood supply can contain. The inflammatory response escalates, pressure builds within the pulp chamber — bounded by rigid dentine walls — and eventually the circulatory system can no longer perfuse the tissue [1]. The transition from reversible to irreversible is a continuum, not a sharp step [1].

The anatomy of primary teeth accelerates this process: enamel is only ~1 mm thick, pulp horns are large and close to the surface [2], and the thin accessory canals at the furcation mean infection escapes to the inter-radicular bone early [3].
problems.presentation:
The parent reports the child is waking at night in pain, or refusing meals. The child may hold the cheek on the affected side or refuse to bite on that side.

What you will see:

- A large carious lesion, often with marginal ridge breakdown [4].
- Tooth may or may not be tender to gentle percussion.
- No swelling or sinus at this stage (that would indicate abscess progression).
- Child's pain report: longer-lasting pain on hot/cold stimulus, or spontaneous pain with no initiating factor [5].
problems.results:
- **Sensibility testing**: unreliable in primary teeth [6].
- **Percussion**: may be positive but often equivocal.
- **Mobility**: normal unless the furcation is also involved.
- **Radiograph**: may show no inter-radicular radiolucency yet, or an early ill-defined radiolucency at the furcation. No clear periapical lucency if the pulp is not yet fully necrotic. Bitewings show extent of caries; if no clear separation between the caries and the pulp canal is visible, pulpotomy should be considered [7].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
Unlike reversible pulpitis, the pain does not settle quickly and often has a spontaneous element [5]. Unlike a periapical abscess, there is no swelling, sinus, or frank mobility from periradicular bone destruction.

The three stages — reversible pulpitis → irreversible pulpitis → abscess — are on a continuum. Clinicians must decide which stage applies, using clinical judgement rather than a clean diagnostic threshold [1]. For multi-rooted primary molars, individual root canals can be at different stages simultaneously [8].
problems.treatment:
**Pulpotomy** is the treatment of choice for a cooperative child where the pulp can still be maintained radicular to the chamber floor [9]:

- Give LA and place rubber dam.
- Complete cavity preparation and remove caries.
- Remove roof of pulp chamber; amputate coronal pulp with a large excavator or sterile round bur.
- Wash chamber and arrest bleeding with damp cotton wool.
- Place cotton wool pledget dampened with **15.5% ferric sulfate** on exposed pulp stumps for at least 1 minute, then remove. Alternatively place CaOH or MTA over root stumps once bleeding is arrested [10].
- Apply ZOE cement dressing.
- Restore with a stainless steel crown (SS crown gives superior longevity over plastic restorations) [10].

If the child is uncooperative: extraction, or temporary dressing and review [9]. If pulpotomy is not feasible and the tooth cannot be extracted due to bleeding disorders or other medical reasons, refer for specialist assessment [11].
problems.prognosis:
Pulpotomy with ferric sulfate: success rate 70–90% [12]. Formocresol historically similar but no longer first choice. With successful pulpotomy, the tooth is kept until natural exfoliation.

Without treatment, irreversible pulpitis progresses to pulp necrosis and periapical/inter-radicular infection. A non-vital tooth with inter-radicular radiolucency is managed by pulpectomy or extraction — pulpotomy is no longer appropriate at that stage [13].

citations.quote: Eventually, the bacterial infection and the associated increase in tissue pressure overwhelms the ability of the circulatory system to keep the pulp perfused, which will then transition from being vital (perfused), to non-vital and necrotic (no perfusion). Clinically, it is useful to divide this process into three stages: pulpitis with reversible symptoms, pulpitis with irreversible symptoms and dental abscess/periradicular periodontitis. However, these do not refer to discrete, well separated stages of pathology, but are on a continuum of unmanaged pulpal disease.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children — Causes of dental pain or infection

These features mean that caries will affect the pulp sooner and there is a greater likelihood of pulp exposure during cavity preparation.

citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1332

citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1350

citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1127

citations.source: IADT Guidelines — Injuries in the primary dentition, §1.5

citations.quote: For primary molars, where a radiograph shows no clear separation between the carious lesion and the dental pulp, consider carrying out a pulpotomy.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children — Managing dental pain or infection

citations.quote: For a child in pain due to pulpitis in a vital primary tooth with irreversible symptoms and no evidence of dental abscess, consider carrying out a pulpotomy to preserve the tooth and to avoid the need for an extraction. (Conditional recommendation; moderate certainty evidence)

citations.quote: Place cotton wool pledget dampened with 15.5% ferric sulfate on exposed pulp stumps for at least 1min, then remove. Alternatively, once bleeding arrested, place CaOH or MTA over root stumps. Apply dressing of reinforced zinc oxide eugenol (ZOE) cement. Restore tooth, usually with a stainless steel crown.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraphs 1563–1565 (pulpotomy technique)

citations.quote: Any medical condition where a focus of infection is potentially dangerous is a C/I to pulp therapy. Pulp therapy may be preferable to extraction in children with bleeding disorders.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraphs 1528–1529 (indications and contraindications for pulp therapy)

citations.quote: Formocresol—historically widely used for 1° teeth pulpotomy, because of its ease of use and high success rate (70–90%). Ferric sulfate—the technique recommended by many authorities as an alternative to formocresol. Success rates have been shown to nearly match formocresol.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraphs 1551–1552 (pulpotomy materials)

citations.quote: Necrotic pulp (i.e. no bleeding)—proceed with non-vital technique or extract.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1569 (pulpotomy problems)

problems.description: A small blister or pimple on the gum above or below a child's back tooth, sometimes with facial swelling. The child may or may not report pain.
problems.conditionName: Dentoalveolar abscess from a primary tooth
problems.etiology:
Pulp necrosis allows bacteria to proliferate in the root canal system. The bacteria and their products diffuse through the radicular foramina, causing inflammation of the periodontal ligament [1]. Because primary molar roots are flared to straddle the developing premolar, and the pulpal floor has accessory canals opening to the furcation, infection typically tracks inter-radicularly rather than periapically — a characteristic pattern unique to primary molars [2].

This is almost always a consequence of unmanaged caries. The continuum from caries through pulpitis to necrosis and abscess can occur silently: it is possible for the pulp to become completely necrotic without any symptoms the child reports [3].
problems.presentation:
The parent brings the child because they noticed 'a spot on the gum' or 'a swelling on the face'. The child may have no pain if the abscess is chronic and draining, or acute severe pain with facial swelling if it is not.

What you will see:

- A sinus (parulis) on the non-attached mucosa adjacent to the attached gingiva, often buccal to the affected tooth [4].
- A slight cleft or notch in the adjacent gingival margin may be present [4].
- Alveolar swelling or tenderness on palpation adjacent to the tooth.
- Non-physiological mobility when the tooth is gently rocked bucco-lingually with tweezers placed on the occlusal surface [4].
- Facial swelling in acute cases.
- A large carious tooth, often deeply broken down.
problems.results:
- **Percussion**: tender, but may be equivocal in young children.
- **Mobility**: increased, non-physiological (compare with the healthy contralateral tooth) [4].
- **Radiograph**: inter-radicular radiolucency is the characteristic sign — a radiolucency in the furcation area of a primary molar, visible on bitewing or periapical films [4, 2]. Periapical radiolucency less common than inter-radicular in primary molars.
- **Sinus probing**: a gutta-percha point placed into the sinus and radiographed will trace back to the infected tooth.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The key distinguishing feature of primary molar abscess is the **inter-radicular radiolucency**, not periapical — because infection tracks through the thin pulpal floor and accessory furcation canals rather than down the root to the apex [2].

Compare to:

- **Non-physiological mobility from exfoliation**: the permanent successor is visible radiographically, root resorption is advancing, no inter-radicular radiolucency.
- **Periodontal abscess**: uncommon in primary dentition; would show pocket formation rather than inter-radicular bone loss.
- **Infection after trauma**: history of trauma rather than caries, may involve upper incisors.
problems.treatment:
Dental infection must not be left untreated [5].

**Primary teeth with abscess:**

- **Extraction** is usually the best option and the most straightforward in primary care [6].
- In certain circumstances, **referral for pulpectomy** is appropriate — particularly when the tooth is important for space maintenance, the child has a bleeding disorder, or is otherwise medically complex [6].

**Pulpectomy technique** (if retained tooth is justified):

- LA and rubber dam; remove necrotic pulp; locate, file, and irrigate canals (sodium hypochlorite 0.1%) [7].
- Cleanse to within 2–3 mm of the apex; do not extend beyond.
- Fill with plain ZOE paste, non-setting calcium hydroxide, or iodoform paste (e.g. Vitapex®) — a resorbable material is essential so the filling resorbs with the root [7].
- Restore with SS crown. Arrange clinical and radiographic review [7].

**Antibiotics**: not recommended unless there are signs of spreading infection or systemic involvement [5]. It is unacceptable to use antibiotics as a substitute for definitive treatment.

If the child is pre-cooperative or infection becomes symptomatic acutely and the child cannot tolerate treatment: consider referral for sedation or GA [5].
problems.prognosis:
Extraction: predictably resolves the infection. The space consequence depends on which tooth and the child's age — early loss of a first primary molar or canine in a crowded case can cause space loss and centre-line shift [8].

Successful pulpectomy: success rate >80% at 3 years [9]. An important advantage is space maintenance for the permanent successor.

In >50% of children under 4 years of age, trauma or infection of a primary incisor can affect the developing permanent successor [10]; similarly, inter-radicular infection spreading to the underlying premolar crypt is a known risk of prolonged abscesses in primary molars.

citations.quote: Bacteria can then thrive within the necrotic pulpal remnants, and the diffusion of these bacteria and their products through the radicular foramina causes inflammation of the periodontal ligament (hence these teeth becoming tender to percussion and mobile), and a dental abscess.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children — Causes of dental pain or infection

citations.quote: Thin pulpal floor and accessory canals. This may explain the greater incidence of inter-radicular involvement following pulp death.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1332

citations.quote: It is possible for pulpal disease to progress from mild inflammation to complete pulpal necrosis without any obvious signs, and without the child reporting symptoms.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children — Causes of dental pain or infection

citations.quote: Dental abscess/infection can be difficult to diagnose because the clinical presentation can vary. Sinuses, if present, are not always obvious, but they are usually located on the non-attached mucosa adjacent to the attached mucosa. A slight cleft or notch may also be seen in the adjacent gingival margin. Look for the following indicators of established dental infection: tenderness to percussion in a non-exfoliating tooth; alveolar tenderness, sinus or swelling; non-physiological mobility (compared with the healthy contralateral tooth) when the tooth is gently rocked bucco-lingually with the points of a pair of tweezers placed on the occlusal surface; radiographic signs including inter-radicular radiolucency.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children — Assessing for dental abscess/infection in primary teeth

citations.quote: Do not leave dental infection untreated. Antibiotics are not recommended unless there are signs of spreading infection or systemic symptoms.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children — Managing dental pain or infection

citations.quote: Manage a primary tooth which is associated with infection (signs or symptoms of abscess, sinus, inter-radicular radiolucency, non-physiological mobility) either by extraction or, in certain circumstances consider referral for pulpectomy.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children — Management of caries in primary teeth

citations.quote: Remove the necrotic pulp, locate and file and irrigate canals (sodium hypochlorite 0.1%). Cleanse to within 2–3mm of apex, but avoid extending beyond. Fill canal with plain ZOE paste, non-setting calcium hydroxide, or iodoform paste (e.g. Vitapex®) with a spiral filler. Restore with SS crown. Arrange clinical and radiographic review.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraphs 1574–1578 (pulpectomy technique)

citations.quote: Although early loss of 1° incisors will have little effect, extraction of C, D, or E will, in a crowded case, lead to localization of the crowding.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1352

citations.quote: A success rate of >80% at 3yrs has been reported.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1581 (pulpectomy success rate)

citations.quote: In >50% of children <4yrs, trauma to a 1° tooth affects the underlying developing successor. The effect depends upon stage of development, type of injury and severity, Rx, and pulpal sequelae. Trauma can cause hypomineralization, hypoplasia, dilaceration, severe malformation, and arrest of development.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1686

problems.description: A toddler's front tooth has been pushed up into the gum after a fall — it has almost or completely disappeared into the socket.
problems.conditionName: Intrusive luxation of a primary incisor
problems.etiology:
Primary incisor intrusion is the most common traumatic dental injury in young children — intrusion accounts for over 60% of primary tooth injuries [1]. The mechanism is a direct axial force on the crown, usually from a fall at toddler age when children are learning to walk and run. The force drives the tooth into the alveolus.

Alveolar bone is more elastic in young children, meaning less fracture and more luxation on impact [2]. The root of the primary incisor has a close spatial relationship to the underlying permanent incisor tooth germ, so the direction of displacement determines whether the permanent successor is at risk [3].
problems.presentation:
The parent arrives acutely after a witnessed fall. The upper front tooth (usually a central or lateral incisor) is not visible or appears shorter than usual. The gingiva around it looks bruised or swollen. There may be associated lip laceration.

The tooth can usually be palpated labially as a hard ridge beneath the mucosa [4]. The child may be distressed; careful knee-to-knee examination is helpful [5].
problems.results:
- **Radiograph (essential)**: a periapical or occlusal view is taken to determine the direction of displacement.
  - If the apex is displaced toward the **labial bone plate**: the image of the tooth appears foreshortened and the apical tip is visible [4].
  - If the apex is displaced **toward the permanent tooth germ**: the image appears elongated (the root has moved palatal-apically) [4].
- **Sensibility testing**: unreliable in primary teeth; not recommended [6].
- Note tooth colour and mobility at this visit and each follow-up: crown discoloration is a common subsequent complication [7].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
Intrusion is distinct from avulsion (tooth completely out of the socket) and from subluxation (mobile but not displaced).

The direction-of-displacement question is clinically critical: intrusion toward the labial bone plate is more favourable for the permanent tooth than intrusion driving the primary apex into the tooth germ. The 2020 IADT guidelines no longer recommend immediate extraction based on displacement direction alone — evidence supports waiting for spontaneous re-eruption [3].

Unlike permanent tooth intrusion (where active repositioning is advised based on apex status and depth), in primary teeth the first-line management is **observation** in most cases [3, 8].
problems.treatment:
The IADT 2020 position [3, 8]:

- Allow the tooth to **spontaneously reposition itself**, irrespective of the direction of displacement.
- Spontaneous improvement usually occurs within 6 months; in some cases up to 1 year [8].
- Arrange **rapid referral within a couple of days** to a child-oriented team with experience in paediatric dental injuries.
- Extraction is indicated if: the tooth fails to re-erupt within the expected window, or signs of infection develop (sinus, swelling, inter-radicular radiolucency on X-ray).

**Homecare instructions** for parents [9]:

- Soft diet; encourage return to normal function as soon as possible.
- Clean the area with a soft brush and alcohol-free chlorhexidine gluconate 0.1–0.2% mouth rinse topically twice daily for 1 week.
- Watch for warning signs: gingival swelling, sinus tract, or persistent dark discoloration of the crown.

Pulpal necrosis often follows intrusive luxation of primary teeth — if it occurs, either RCT or extraction is needed [1].
problems.prognosis:
If the tooth re-erupts without developing infection: favourable. Many teeth regain near-normal position. A transient red/grey or yellow discoloration may occur; yellow discoloration suggests pulp canal obliteration — no treatment required if the tooth is asymptomatic [7].

Persistent dark grey discoloration with any sign of infection — sinus, swelling, radiographic lucency — indicates pulp necrosis; treat or extract [7].

Damage to the permanent successor is the major long-term risk. Intrusion and avulsion injuries are most commonly associated with developmental anomalies in the permanent dentition [3]. Parents must be warned of this risk at the first visit [3].

citations.quote: Most common injury (>60%). Unfortunately, pulpal necrosis often follows, necessitating either pulp Rx or extraction.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1669 (intrusion of primary incisor)

citations.quote: About 30–40% of 5yr-olds have experienced dental trauma, most frequently at toddler stage. As alveolar bone is more elastic the younger the child, the most common injuries are luxation or avulsion. Crown and root # are relatively rare.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1658

citations.quote: There is a close spatial relationship between the apex of the primary tooth root and the underlying permanent tooth germ. Intrusion and avulsion injuries are most commonly associated with the development of anomalies in the permanent dentition. For intrusive and lateral luxation injuries, previous Guidelines have recommended the immediate extraction of the traumatized primary tooth if the direction of displacement of the root is toward the permanent tooth germ. This action is no longer advised due to (a) evidence of spontaneous re-eruption for intruded primary teeth.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines — Injuries in the primary dentition, §1.8

citations.quote: The tooth has almost or completely disappeared into the socket and can be palpated labially. When the apex is displaced toward or through the labial bone plate, the apical tip can be seen and the image of the tooth will appear shorter (foreshortened) than the contralateral tooth. When the apex is displaced toward the permanent tooth germ, the apical tip cannot be visualized and the image of the tooth will appear elongated.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines — Injuries in the primary dentition, Table 11 (intrusive luxation)

citations.quote: At this young age, the child may resist co-operating for an extensive examination, radiographs, and treatment. Knee-to-knee examination can be helpful in examining a young child.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines — Injuries in the primary dentition, §1.1

citations.quote: Pulp sensibility tests are unreliable in primary teeth and are therefore not recommended.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines — Injuries in the primary dentition, §1.5

citations.quote: The color of injured and uninjured teeth should be recorded at each clinic visit. Discoloration is a common complication following luxation injuries. Teeth with persistent dark discoloration may remain asymptomatic clinically and radiographically normal, or they may develop apical periodontitis (with or without symptoms). Root canal treatment is not indicated for discolored teeth unless there are clinical or radiographic signs of infection of the root canal system.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines — Injuries in the primary dentition, §1.5

citations.quote: The tooth should be allowed to spontaneously reposition itself, irrespective of the direction of displacement. Spontaneous improvement in the position of the intruded tooth usually occurs within 6 mo. In some cases, it can take up to 1 y.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines — Injuries in the primary dentition, Table 11 (intrusive luxation — treatment)

citations.quote: To encourage gingival healing and prevent plaque accumulation, parents should clean the affected area with a soft brush or cotton swab combined with an alcohol-free 0.1%-0.2% chlorhexidine gluconate mouth rinse applied topically twice a day for 1 wk.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines — Injuries in the primary dentition, §1.12

problems.description: A primary tooth has been completely knocked out of its socket after a fall — the child's parent is asking whether to put it back.
problems.etiology:
Avulsion (complete displacement of a tooth from its socket) results from a traumatic impact strong enough to tear the periodontal ligament entirely. It is less common than intrusion in primary teeth; the elastic alveolar bone of young children tends to yield to luxation rather than complete avulsion [1].

The immediate clinical concern is twofold: the tooth itself, and what the avulsion means for the developing permanent tooth germ lying in close proximity to the root apex [2].
problems.presentation:
Parent presents with a child who has lost a front tooth acutely. They often bring the tooth and want to know if it can be replanted. The socket is visible, empty, and bleeding. There may be associated soft tissue injuries to the lip, gingivae, or frenulum.

If the tooth is not found: the child must be referred for medical evaluation including chest X-ray to exclude aspiration — this applies particularly if the accident was unwitnessed or there are respiratory symptoms [3].
problems.results:
- **Radiograph (essential when tooth not brought to clinic)**: to confirm the tooth has not been intruded rather than avulsed. The radiograph also provides a baseline for assessing the developing permanent tooth germ [3].
- **Clinical examination**: empty socket, assessment of soft tissue injuries, any other teeth displaced or fractured.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The defining management difference from permanent tooth avulsion: **do not replant a primary tooth** [3, 4].

The reasons:

- Replantation of a primary tooth risks further damage to the underlying permanent tooth germ during the procedure itself [4].
- It requires splinting, multiple appointments, and root canal treatment — a significant treatment burden for a very young child [4].
- The most important safety reason: risk of aspiration during replantation in a young, uncooperative child [4].

This is the sharpest primary vs. permanent distinction in paediatric trauma — the IADT guidelines are explicit. Replantation is the gold standard for permanent teeth but is **contraindicated** for primary teeth.
problems.treatment:
- **Do not replant** the avulsed primary tooth [3, 4].
- **Reassure** the parents that the permanent tooth will still erupt in due course.
- Provide homecare instructions: soft diet; clean the area with alcohol-free chlorhexidine gluconate 0.12% mouth rinse on a soft brush or cotton swab twice daily for 1 week [5].
- **Clinical review at 6–8 weeks** to monitor healing and assess for any injury to the permanent successor [3].
- **Follow up at 6 years of age** (or whenever permanent incisors are expected to erupt) to monitor eruption of the permanent tooth [3].
- Document: inform parents in writing of the risk of developmental anomalies in the permanent successor [2].
problems.prognosis:
The socket heals. The permanent incisor will usually erupt normally, but avulsion — like intrusion — is most commonly associated with developmental anomalies in the permanent dentition [2]. The spectrum of possible effects on the permanent tooth includes: hypomineralisation, hypoplasia, dilaceration, severe malformation, and arrest of development [6].

Parents must be warned of this risk, and follow-up arranged until the permanent successor has erupted.

citations.quote: As alveolar bone is more elastic the younger the child, the most common injuries are luxation or avulsion. Crown and root # are relatively rare.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1658

citations.quote: There is a close spatial relationship between the apex of the primary tooth root and the underlying permanent tooth germ. Intrusion and avulsion injuries are most commonly associated with the development of anomalies in the permanent dentition. It is very important to document that parents have been informed about possible complications to the development of the permanent teeth, especially following intrusion, avulsion, and alveolar fractures.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines — Injuries in the primary dentition, §1.8

citations.quote: Avulsed primary teeth should not be replanted. A periapical or occlusal radiograph is essential where the primary tooth is not brought into the clinic to ensure that the missing tooth has not been intruded. The radiograph will also provide a baseline for assessment of the developing permanent tooth and to determine whether it has been displaced. Clinical examination after 6-8 wk. Further follow up at 6 y of age is indicated to monitor eruption of the permanent tooth.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines — Injuries in the primary dentition, Table 12 (avulsion)

citations.quote: An avulsed primary tooth should not be replanted. Reasons include a significant treatment burden (including replantation, splint placement and removal, root canal treatment) for a young child as well as the potential of causing further damage to the permanent tooth or to its eruption. However, the most important reason is to avoid a medical emergency resulting from aspiration of the tooth.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines — Injuries in the primary dentition, §1.10

citations.quote: To encourage gingival healing and prevent plaque accumulation, parents should clean the affected area with a soft brush or cotton swab combined with an alcohol-free 0.1%-0.2% chlorhexidine gluconate mouth rinse applied topically twice a day for 1 wk.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines — Injuries in the primary dentition, §1.12

citations.quote: In >50% of children <4yrs, trauma to a 1° tooth affects the underlying developing successor. The effect depends upon stage of development, type of injury and severity, Rx, and pulpal sequelae. Trauma can cause hypomineralization, hypoplasia (likelihood ↑ if <4yrs &/or injury more severe), dilaceration, severe malformation, and arrest of development.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1686

problems.description: A primary molar sits visibly lower than the teeth on either side, below the occlusal plane, sometimes appearing to be slowly 'sinking' into the gum.
problems.etiology:
Ankylosis of a primary molar results from disruption of the normal resorptive–repair cycle during exfoliation — the root becomes fused to the alveolar bone, losing its periodontal ligament space at that point [1]. The tooth cannot migrate occlusally with the growing alveolus, so it appears to sink as the adjacent teeth continue erupting.

The condition is often self-correcting when a permanent successor is erupting normally — the successor's eruption force contributes to root resorption and eventually the ankylosed tooth exfoliates [1].
problems.presentation:
The parent may notice the child's tooth looks shorter than the others, or the child may have reported food packing in the gap. Often found incidentally on clinical exam or radiograph.

What you will see:

- The primary molar sits below the occlusal level of adjacent teeth [1].
- Adjacent teeth may be tipping into the space.
- A hard, hollow percussion note ('dull thud') compared with adjacent teeth — the ankylosis replaces the PDL's shock-absorbing properties. This is clinically distinct from the normal percussion note.
- No mobility (ankylosed tooth).
problems.results:
- **Radiograph**: loss of the normal PDL space at the site of ankylosis; the tooth appears fused to the alveolar bone at that point.
- Look for: the position and development of the permanent premolar successor. If the premolar is missing or ectopic, or the molar is sinking below contact with adjacent teeth, active management is indicated [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The infraoccluded primary molar is usually self-correcting when the permanent successor is present and in a good position. The intervention threshold is [1]:

- Permanent successor is **missing or ectopic** (no eruption force to resorb the root).
- The molar is sinking **below the contact area** with adjacent teeth (space loss becoming a clinical problem).
- The molar is **approaching or below the gingival level** (the tooth is 'disappearing').

The reason for concern when the premolar is absent: an ankylosed tooth without a successor will sit in bone indefinitely as a submerged unit, potentially causing the adjacent teeth to tip significantly and complicate later prosthetic or orthodontic treatment.
problems.treatment:
- If the permanent successor is present and not ectopic, and the tooth is not sinking below contact: **observe and monitor carefully** [1].
- If any of the intervention criteria are met: **extract the ankylosed tooth**. Any resulting space loss is dealt with as part of the overall orthodontic plan [1].
- If in doubt: **specialist opinion** [1].
problems.prognosis:
When the premolar is present: the ankylosed molar usually exfoliates at the expected time, albeit with variable amounts of tipping of adjacent teeth. Space loss is the main sequela to manage.

When the premolar is absent: the ankylosed molar may persist indefinitely; the adjacent teeth tip progressively into the space. Early extraction and space management is preferred to late discovery of a severely tipped arch.

citations.quote: These occur where the 1° molar has failed to maintain its position relevant to the adjacent teeth in the developing dentition and is therefore below the occlusal level of adjacent teeth. Often due to ankylosis 2° to disruption in normal resorptive/repair cycle of exfoliation. This is usually self-correcting (if the permanent successor is present and not ectopic) and the affected tooth is exfoliated at the normal time. However, where the premolar is missing or ectopic, where the infraoccluded molar moves below the contact of adjacent teeth, or appears in danger of disappearing below the gingival level, extraction may be indicated (monitor carefully and if in doubt get a specialist opinion).
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1160 (infraoccluded/ankylosed primary molars)

problems.description: A tooth is present in a newborn's mouth at birth, causing feeding difficulty or a raw ulcer on the underside of the infant's tongue.
problems.etiology: Teeth present at birth. Most are members of the primary dentition — lower incisor region is the usual site [1]. The thing is, at birth these teeth have had very little time to develop root structure, so limited root development is the rule at that stage [1].
problems.presentation: A tooth or teeth visible in the mouth at the newborn examination. Parents or midwives raise the concern. Most frequently the lower incisor region [1]. The tooth may be mobile because of its limited root development [1].
problems.results:
- **Clinical assessment**: determine tooth mobility — high mobility raises the aspiration risk.
- **Radiograph**: confirms whether it is a primary tooth or supernumerary, and shows the extent of root development. A supernumerary natal tooth can be removed without consequence; a primary tooth removal has space implications.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Natal teeth are present at birth; **neonatal teeth** erupt within the first 30 days of life — the distinction is timing, not pathology. The two key management questions are: is the tooth a member of the normal primary series or a supernumerary, and is it mobile enough to present an aspiration risk [1]?
problems.treatment:
Retain if possible — most natal teeth are primary incisors and early loss has space implications [1]. The goal is to preserve the tooth unless retention is unsafe.

- If **in danger of being inhaled** (high mobility) or causing **significant breastfeeding difficulties**: remove. The procedure can usually be done with topical LA alone or no anaesthesia at all [1].
problems.prognosis: Removal of a mobile natal tooth resolves aspiration risk.

citations.quote: Usually members of the 1° dentition, can sometimes be supernumerary, and should be retained if possible. Most frequently occur in lower incisor region and because of limited root development at that age, are often mobile. If in danger of being inhaled or causing problems with breastfeeding, they can be removed (usually removed with no LA or some topical LA is applied).
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1137 (natal teeth)

problems.description: An infant or toddler is unsettled, drooling, and difficult to settle at night — no obvious dental lesion on inspection.
problems.etiology: The eruption of primary teeth coincides with a natural drop in circulating maternal antibodies, so the period is often blamed for systemic symptoms. The thing is, the honest picture is more modest: what the source actually supports is local gingival discomfort and disturbed sleep accompanying the eruption process itself [1]. Systemic attribution (fever, diarrhoea) is not well supported [1].
problems.presentation: Infant is irritable, drooling, and sleeping poorly. Parents may report gnawing behaviour and sore-looking gums. On inspection: erythema and slight swelling of the gingiva overlying the erupting tooth is the typical finding. No caries, no sinus, no swelling [1].
problems.results: Diagnosis is clinical. No investigations are required. The key role of the examination is to exclude other pathology — caries, eruption cyst, or early infection — that might be attributed to teething.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The reason teething sits apart from other entries in this origin is that it is physiological, not pathological. Local gum discomfort is real and source-supported; systemic symptoms traditionally blamed on teething (fevers, diarrhoea) are not [1]. If a child appears systemically unwell, look for another cause rather than defaulting to teething.
problems.treatment:
Symptomatic relief is the goal [1]:

- Proprietary teething preparations containing a combination of analgesic, antiseptic, and anti-inflammatory agents for topical use [1].
- Something firm to chew: a teething ring. Designs that can be cooled in the fridge may enhance the soothing effect [1].
- Reassure parents: this is self-limiting.
problems.prognosis: Self-limiting by definition. Each tooth erupts and symptoms resolve. No treatment is required beyond symptomatic relief.

citations.quote: As eruption of the 1° dentition coincides with a diminution in circulating maternal antibodies, teething is often blamed for systemic symptoms. However, local discomfort, and so disturbed sleep, may accompany the actual process of eruption. A number of proprietary 'teething' preparations are available, which usually contain a combination of an analgesic, an antiseptic, and anti-inflammatory agents for topical use. Having something hard to chew may help, e.g. teething ring. Some are designed to be cooled in the fridge, which can enhance their soothing ability.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1139 (teething)

problems.description: A soft, bluish swelling on the gum over an unerupted tooth in a young child — no pain, the tooth beneath it has not yet broken through.
problems.etiology: Fluid or blood accumulates in the follicular space overlying an erupting tooth before the crown breaks through the mucosa [1]. When blood is the main constituent, the swelling takes on a bluish hue [1].
problems.presentation: A soft, fluctuant, dome-shaped swelling in the alveolar mucosa overlying a tooth that is about to erupt. Colour ranges from normal pink to bluish-purple depending on how much blood is in the follicular fluid [1]. No tenderness to light palpation in most cases. The child is typically of an age consistent with eruption of the affected tooth. Parents are usually the ones who notice it — the child rarely reports symptoms.
problems.results: Diagnosis is clinical. No radiograph is required unless the eruption seems significantly delayed or the presentation is atypical.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The bluish swelling over an erupting tooth is the defining picture. What distinguishes this from a true dentigerous cyst or from a haemangioma is context: it arises specifically over an erupting tooth, in a child at the expected age for that tooth to emerge, and it resolves spontaneously once the tooth breaks through [1]. No treatment is normally needed [1].
problems.treatment:
Most rupture spontaneously, allowing eruption to proceed without any intervention [1]. The goal is to wait. Reassure the parents.

Rarely, if the swelling is enlarging, the tooth appears stuck, or the child is significantly distressed: marsupialise the cyst. This is a simple incision to decompress the fluid and allow the crown through [1]. No further treatment is required once the tooth has erupted.
problems.prognosis: Excellent. Spontaneous resolution is the rule [1]. Marsupialization is effective on the rare occasion it is needed. No long-term sequelae.

citations.quote: This is caused by an accumulation of fluid or blood in the follicular space overlying an erupting tooth. The presence of blood gives a bluish hue. Most rupture spontaneously, allowing eruption to proceed. Rarely, it may be necessary to marsupialize the cyst.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1141 (eruption cyst)

problems.description: A young child loses a primary tooth unusually early — without extensive caries or trauma to explain it.
problems.conditionName: Premature exfoliation of primary teeth (systemic causes)
problems.etiology:
The most common reason for early tooth loss in any child is extraction for caries, and traumatic avulsion is the next most common. What makes this entry different is loss without an obvious local cause. Systemic disease — neutropenia, leukaemia — can result in an abnormal periodontal attachment, causing premature tooth loss [1]. Hypophosphatasia, a metabolic disorder affecting cementum formation, is a rarer but important cause: aplasia of cementum means the tooth has no structural anchor in the PDL, so even the mildest forces detach it [2].

Alveolar bone loss in a young child is a serious finding [1]. The thing is, the differential includes diseases that need urgent investigation.
problems.presentation:
Parents report that a tooth 'fell out' without apparent cause, or with minimal provocation. The child is younger than expected for exfoliation of that tooth. There may be multiple teeth affected.

Systemic symptoms — recurrent infections, pallor, fatigue, easy bruising — may point to neutropenia or leukaemia and must be actively sought [1].
problems.results:
- **Radiograph**: the key finding is absence of the normal physiological root resorption pattern — the root may be intact or only minimally resorbed, confirming this is not natural exfoliation.
- Urgent referral is warranted when alveolar bone loss is identified in a young child [1].
- In hypophosphatasia: premature exfoliation is the result of cementum aplasia [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: What separates this from normal exfoliation is the absence of physiological root resorption, the young age of the child, and the lack of an adequate local cause [1]. Neutropenia and leukaemia present with systemic features; hypophosphatasia is diagnosed by the biochemical marker (low alkaline phosphatase) and cementum aplasia on the extracted tooth [2]. Alveolar bone loss on radiograph in a young child is not a normal finding — it warrants urgent referral regardless of which systemic condition is suspected [1].
problems.treatment: Urgent referral is the action, not a dental restoration [1]. Once a systemic cause is identified, management is led by the appropriate medical team.
problems.prognosis: Depends entirely on the underlying diagnosis.

citations.quote: The most common reason for early tooth loss is extraction for caries. Traumatic avulsion is less common. More rarely, systemic disease such as neutropenia or leukaemia may result in an abnormal periodontal attachment and thus premature tooth loss. Alveolar bone loss in a young child is a serious finding and warrants urgent referral.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1164 (premature exfoliation)

citations.quote: Hypoplasia and aplasia of cementum are uncommon. The latter occurs in hypophosphatasia and results in premature exfoliation.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1250 (cementum disturbances)

problems.description: Chalky, opaque or discoloured patches on a child's second primary molar — the surface breaks down soon after the tooth erupts, and the tooth is painfully sensitive.
problems.etiology: A developmental defect of dental enamel — the mineralisation of the enamel matrix is disturbed during crown formation, producing enamel that is softer and more porous than normal [1]. HSPM shares features with molar-incisor hypomineralisation (MIH) of the permanent dentition. The interesting bit: HSPM is now recognised as a predictor that MIH may be more likely to occur in the permanent dentition [1].
problems.presentation: Chalky white, cream, yellow, or brown opacities on one or more second primary molars. Typically noticed when the molars erupt. The affected enamel often fractures under normal occlusal load shortly after eruption (post-eruptive breakdown) [1]. Secondary caries progression is a known consequence [1]. The child may be very reluctant to allow examination or brushing of the area.
problems.results:
- **Clinical examination**: demarcated opacities on the second primary molar — the key finding is that the opacity is **demarcated** (sharp boundary with normal enamel) rather than diffuse.
- **Post-eruptive breakdown**: chipped or missing enamel in the opacity zone, with exposed dentine.
- **Secondary caries**: the softened enamel is highly susceptible to carious attack and caries progression [1].
- Sensibility testing: unreliable in primary teeth.
problems.definingCharacteristics: HSPM is a developmental defect, not a carious process: the opacity is present from the moment of eruption. The link to MIH in the permanent dentition is a reason to monitor the first permanent molars carefully as they erupt [1].
problems.treatment: The goal is to prevent secondary caries, which HSPM predisposes to [1]. Monitor the permanent dentition: HSPM predicts a higher likelihood of MIH in the permanent teeth [1].
problems.prognosis: The signal value of HSPM for the permanent dentition is the more important long-term consideration: arrange follow-up to assess the first permanent molars at eruption [1].

citations.quote: HSPM is a developmental defect of dental enamel that shares features with MIH. Also known as 1° molar hypomineralization. It may lead to post-eruptive breakdown and 2° caries. Recent studies suggest it is a predictor that MIH may be more likely to occur in the permanent dentition.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1231 (hypomineralised second primary molars)

problems.description: A child's tooth looks unusually wide or doubled — two crowns, or a single crown much wider than the tooth on the other side.
problems.etiology: Two distinct mechanisms produce the same clinical appearance. **Gemination** occurs by partial splitting of a single tooth germ, producing a wide or bifid crown from one root [1]. **Fusion** occurs when two separate tooth germs merge [2]. Fusion can involve two teeth from the normal series, or — less commonly — a normal tooth and a supernumerary [2]. So counting the total number of teeth in the arch will not always reveal the correct mechanism: a fused tooth that includes a supernumerary still leaves the tooth count normal [2].
problems.presentation: A tooth that is noticeably wider than its counterpart on the other side, or a tooth with an obvious groove down the crown suggesting two joined crowns. The condition affects both primary and permanent dentitions [3]. The parent may notice the unusual shape when the tooth erupts.
problems.results:
- **Clinical examination**: wide or bifid crown. A deep groove or cleft running down the centre of the crown is a common finding.
- **Radiograph**: determines whether one or two pulp chambers and root canals are present — this drives treatment planning. If separate pulp chambers exist, separation may be possible; if a single chamber exists, separation risks pulp exposure.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The distinction between gemination (one germ, split) and fusion (two germs, joined) is, as the source notes, really only of academic interest — the clinical management is the same [3]. The term **double teeth** covers both. In primary teeth, the main concern is whether the condition affects the tooth count and thus the space available for permanent successors: a fused primary tooth involving a supernumerary may have two permanent successors competing for one space [2].
problems.treatment:
Rx for aesthetics should be delayed to allow pulpal recession [4]. Here's the sequence once the pulp has receded:

- If separate pulp chambers and root canals: surgical separation can be considered [4].
- If fused with a supernumerary: extract the supernumerary component [4].
- If a single shared pulp chamber: the tooth can be contoured to resemble two separate teeth, or the bulk of the crown can be reduced [4].
problems.prognosis: Generally good with appropriate management. Space implications for the permanent dentition depend on whether a supernumerary is involved — counting the total number of teeth in the arch will not always reveal the correct mechanism [2].

citations.quote: This occurs by partial splitting of a tooth germ.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1257 (gemination)

citations.quote: Fusion occurs as a result of the fusion of two tooth germs. As fusion can take place between either two teeth of the normal series or, less commonly, with a $ tooth, then counting the number of teeth will not always give the correct aetiology.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1259 (fusion)

citations.quote: As the distinction is really only of academic interest, the term 'double teeth' is to be preferred. Both 1° and 2° teeth may be affected and a wide variation in presentation is seen. The prevalence in the 2° dentition is 0.1–0.2%.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1260 (double teeth)

citations.quote: Rx for aesthetics should be delayed to allow pulpal recession. If the tooth has separate pulp chambers and root canals, separation can be considered. If it is due to fusion with a $ tooth, the $ portion can be extracted. Where a single pulp chamber exists, sometimes the tooth can be contoured to resemble two separate teeth or the bulk of the crown reduced.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1262 (treatment of double teeth)

problems.description: A non-vital primary molar — already treated or presenting with inter-radicular lucency — where pulpotomy is no longer appropriate.
problems.etiology:
Pulp death in a primary molar follows the same caries-driven continuum as pulpitis, but the pulp has been overwhelmed. Bacteria proliferate in the necrotic tissue, diffuse through radicular foramina and the thin accessory furcation canals, and produce inter-radicular bone destruction [1]. The result is a tooth with no bleeding from the pulp stumps at surgery — confirming non-vitality — and typically some degree of inter-radicular pathology visible radiographically [1].

The complex ribbon-shaped root canal morphology of primary molars makes pulpectomy technically demanding, but it is the treatment of choice when conditions are favourable [2].
problems.presentation: The child may present with a chronic sinus (parulis), recurrent swelling, or be entirely asymptomatic — pulp death can be silent. Often identified incidentally on a radiograph showing inter-radicular radiolucency. A tooth that bled profusely at a pulpotomy attempt — indicating severe radicular inflammation — may also be redirected to pulpectomy or extraction [3].
problems.results:
- **Pulpotomy findings that indicate non-vital technique**: no bleeding from radicular pulp stumps after coronal pulp removal (necrotic pulp) [1], or profuse uncontrollable haemorrhage suggesting more severe inflammation of the radicular pulp [3].
- **Radiograph**: inter-radicular radiolucency, widening of the PDL space, or early pathological root resorption.
- **Clinical**: sinus, mobility, tenderness.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The critical decision point is pulpotomy vs. pulpectomy vs. extraction. Pulpotomy is only appropriate for a tooth with a vital radicular pulp. Once the pulp is necrotic — no bleeding at the pulp stumps — pulpotomy is contraindicated and the options are pulpectomy (if the tooth is worth retaining and conditions allow) or extraction [1]. Pulpectomy in a primary molar requires a resorbable root filling material so it resorbs alongside the root as the permanent successor erupts [4].
problems.treatment:
Here's the sequence for pulpectomy [4, 5]:

- LA and rubber dam.
- Remove necrotic pulp; locate and file canals; irrigate with sodium hypochlorite 0.1%.
- Cleanse to within 2–3 mm of the apex — do not extend beyond.
- If infection is present: two-stage approach, leaving non-setting calcium hydroxide in the canals for 1–2 weeks before filling [6].
- Fill canal with plain ZOE paste, non-setting calcium hydroxide, or iodoform paste (e.g. Vitapex®) — resorbable material is essential [4].
- Restore with SS crown.
- Arrange clinical and radiographic review.

If conditions are unfavourable or the child is uncooperative: extraction.
problems.prognosis: Pulpectomy success rate: >80% at 3 years [7]. Retaining the tooth preserves space for the permanent successor and avoids the need for a space maintainer. Without treatment, the inter-radicular infection will spread and eventually require extraction — at a potentially less favourable time for arch development.

citations.quote: Necrotic pulp (i.e. no bleeding)—proceed with non-vital technique or extract.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1569 (pulpotomy problems)

citations.quote: A pulpectomy is often considered difficult in 1° molars because of the complexity of ribbon-shaped canals (although instrumentation is often easier than some texts might suggest). The risk of damage to the permanent successor also needs to be considered, but if conditions are favourable it is the Rx of choice for non-vital pulps. The technique can be carried out in one or two visits.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1572 (pulpectomy in primary molars)

citations.quote: Profuse haemorrhage—indicates more serious inflammation of the radicular pulp. Intermediate dressing with Ledermix® followed by non-vital technique or extraction.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1570 (pulpotomy: profuse haemorrhage)

citations.quote: Remove the necrotic pulp, locate and file and irrigate canals (sodium hypochlorite 0.1%). Cleanse to within 2–3mm of apex, but avoid extending beyond. Fill canal with plain ZOE paste, non-setting calcium hydroxide, or iodoform paste (e.g. Vitapex®) with a spiral filler. Restore with SS crown. Arrange clinical and radiographic review.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraphs 1574–1578 (pulpectomy technique)

citations.quote: LA and rubber dam.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1573 (pulpectomy: LA and rubber dam)

citations.quote: If there is evidence of any infection a two-stage Rx is recommended, leaving non-setting calcium hydroxide in the canals for 1–2 weeks prior to filling.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1580 (pulpectomy: two-stage Rx)

citations.quote: A success rate of >80% at 3yrs has been reported.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1581 (pulpectomy success rate)

problems.description: A primary front tooth changes colour in the weeks or months after a knock — ranging from a transient pinkish-grey to a persistent dark grey.
problems.conditionName: Post-traumatic discolouration of a primary incisor
problems.etiology: Trauma is followed by discolouration of the primary incisor. The colour and its timing carry diagnostic meaning: early grey/reddish discolouration may be reversible; later grey discolouration indicates pulp necrosis; yellowing suggests calcification [1].
problems.presentation: Parents bring the child back days to weeks after a fall, noticing the tooth has gone grey, pink, or yellow. The child may have no symptoms at all. In some cases the discolouration is first noticed at a routine follow-up appointment [1].
problems.results:
- **Early grey/reddish discolouration**: appearing in the first few days to weeks post-trauma — pulp may still be vital; discolouration potentially reversible [1].
- **Later grey discolouration**: appearing weeks to months after the injury — indicates pulp necrosis [1]. Look for accompanying signs: sinus, swelling, radiographic inter-radicular lucency.
- **Yellow discolouration**: suggests calcification (obliteration) of the pulp canal — no treatment required if the tooth is clinically asymptomatic and radiographically normal [1].
- **Radiograph**: essential at each follow-up. Signs of infection (inter-radicular radiolucency, widening of PDL space) require active treatment regardless of symptoms.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The three-colour rule from the source is the diagnostic framework [1]: early grey/pink = possibly reversible; late grey = necrosis until proven otherwise; yellow = calcification, benign if asymptomatic. The key differentiator for late grey discolouration vs. calcification is the presence or absence of infection signs. Discoloured teeth without infection signs can be monitored and do not require root canal treatment [1].
problems.treatment:
The goal is to distinguish necrosis with infection from calcification or reversible change.

- **Yellow discolouration, no infection signs**: no treatment required [1]. Reassure and monitor.
- **Grey discolouration, no clinical or radiographic infection signs**: monitor; record colour at each visit [1].
- **Grey discolouration with infection signs** (sinus, swelling, inter-radicular lucency): RCT or extraction [1].
problems.prognosis: Early grey/reddish: often resolves without intervention [1]. Established grey with infection: treated by pulpectomy or extraction — the sooner the better to protect the permanent successor. Yellow/calcification: no adverse sequelae anticipated if infection is absent [1].

citations.quote: If tooth becomes grey/reddish in early post-trauma period, pulp may be vital and discoloration reversible. Greying later indicates pulp necrosis. Yellowing of tooth is suggestive of calcification of pulp—no Rx required.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraphs 1679–1680 (post-traumatic discolouration)

problems.description: A primary tooth feels solid and immovable after a knock — it sits below the occlusal level and does not wiggle at all, even years later.
problems.conditionName: Traumatic ankylosis of a primary tooth
problems.etiology: A primary tooth becomes ankylosed after trauma, requiring extraction to prevent displacement of the permanent incisor successor [1].
problems.presentation: History of trauma to the tooth. On examination: no mobility. The tooth may be progressively infraoccluding.
problems.results:
- **Mobility**: absent.
- **Radiograph**: confirm position of the permanent successor.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The defining consequence is displacement of the permanent incisor successor if the ankylosed tooth is not removed [1].
problems.treatment: Extract to prevent displacement of the permanent incisor successor [1]. The goal is to remove the physical obstruction before the permanent tooth has committed to an abnormal eruption path.
problems.prognosis: Extraction prevents displacement of the permanent incisor [1].

citations.quote: Rx: extraction to prevent displacement of 2° incisor.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1682 (traumatic ankylosis of primary tooth)

problems.description: A child's dental midline has shifted to one side, or crowding has worsened, after a primary tooth was extracted earlier than expected.
problems.conditionName: Space loss after premature primary tooth loss
problems.etiology:
When a primary canine or first primary molar is lost early, the adjacent teeth drift into the gap. In a crowded arch, this is the mechanism by which localised crowding escalates into a centre-line discrepancy or blocked permanent teeth [1]. The effect is greatest when: the arch is crowded to start with, the loss is unilateral, and the extraction is of a canine [1].

Unilateral loss of a primary canine is particularly significant. The reason is that in a crowded arch, the contralateral teeth are not lost, so the arch drifts to the extraction side — producing a midline shift that often requires fixed appliances to correct [1].
problems.presentation: The child, or more often the parent, notices that the teeth are not straight. On examination: unilateral space loss or midline shift toward the side of early extraction [1].
problems.results:
- **Clinical examination**: dental midline deviation toward the side of early extraction. Tipping of adjacent teeth.
- **Radiograph**: to assess position of permanent successors and extent of space loss.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The key distinction from normal developmental arch changes is the asymmetry: unilateral space loss producing a centre-line shift is not a normal finding and indicates a specific extraction event [1]. Loss of primary Es causes the first permanent molar to migrate forward — especially marked if the E is lost before the permanent first molar has erupted [1].
problems.treatment:
Prevention is better than cure [1]. Here's the approach:

- **Balancing extraction**: extract the equivalent tooth on the opposite side to preserve symmetry [2].
- **Compensating extraction**: extract the equivalent tooth in the opposing arch [3].
- Loss of primary canines should always be balanced [1].
- If Es are to be extracted: defer until after the permanent first molars are in occlusion where possible, and do not balance or compensate [1].
problems.prognosis: Correction of a centre-line discrepancy often requires fixed appliances [1]. Prevention is better than cure.

citations.quote: Unfortunately, when a child attends with toothache, in the rush to relieve pain it is all too easy to extract the offending tooth without consideration of the consequences. The major effect of early 1° tooth loss is localization of crowding, in crowded mouths. The extent to which this occurs depends upon the patient's age, the degree of crowding, and the site. In a crowded mouth, the adjacent teeth will move round into the extraction space, therefore, unilateral loss of a C (and to a lesser degree a D) will result in a centre-line shift. This is also seen when a C is prematurely exfoliated by an erupting 2. As correction of a centre-line discrepancy often involves FAs, prevention is better than cure, so loss of Cs should always be balanced. If Es are lost, the 6 will migrate forward. This is particularly marked if it occurs before eruption of the permanent tooth, so if extraction of an E is unavoidable try to defer until after the 6s are in occlusion and do not balance or compensate.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 2183 (effects of premature loss of primary teeth)

citations.quote: Extraction of the same (or adjacent) tooth on the opposite side of the arch to preserve symmetry.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 2189 (balancing extraction)

citations.quote: Extraction of the same tooth in the opposing arch.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 2191 (compensating extraction)

problems.description: A very young child loses multiple primary front teeth spontaneously — the teeth appear to fall out with intact roots and no history of trauma or significant caries.
problems.etiology: Hypophosphatasia is a metabolic disorder in which aplasia of cementum results in premature exfoliation [1].
problems.presentation: Multiple primary teeth lost without preceding caries and no relevant trauma. Parents are alarmed by the apparently spontaneous tooth loss.
problems.results: Cementum aplasia is the basis for the premature exfoliation [1]. Further investigation is directed at confirming the systemic diagnosis.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Aplasia of cementum in hypophosphatasia results in premature exfoliation [1]. The condition is uncommon but important to recognise because the metabolic diagnosis has implications beyond the teeth.
problems.treatment: The underlying disorder is systemic. Dental management is supportive.
problems.prognosis: Depends on the severity of the underlying metabolic disorder.

citations.quote: Hypoplasia and aplasia of cementum are uncommon. The latter occurs in hypophosphatasia and results in premature exfoliation.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 1250 (cementum disturbances / hypophosphatasia)
